v0.5.0 taught fufu to rewrite what you already made. This one is about the two ends of that work: seeing what a change actually contains, and getting it out of the machine — plus the two moments before a repository exists, which fufu previously had nothing to say about.

**Sync takes in, publish sends**

This reverses a decision DESIGN.md stated flatly: there is no `ff push` and deliberately never will be, because publishing is the outgoing half of lining up rather than a separate act.

The half of that which held up is that reconciling with the base and reconciling with the remote are the same replay, so one verb covers both. The half that did not is bundling the push in with them. Everything sync does is recorded and reachable from `ff undo`; a push is the one act that leaves the machine, and no operation log reaches across a wire. Putting the single irreversible step inside the verb whose whole promise is reversibility was the tension, and `fufu.pushOnSync` defaulting to true meant it was on unless you opted out.

So `ff sync` is the incoming half and nothing else, and `ff publish` is the outgoing one. The knob is gone from the registry rather than flipped — there is no setting that makes a push happen by itself. Sync ends by naming what is left instead of doing it, and that report is a three-state pending rather than a count: a branch with no shared copy yet has everything to publish, which is not zero commits waiting. A live run against a real remote is what turned that up — the count version printed nothing at all in exactly the open-a-PR case the split was for.

`ff publish` does not fetch, and that is the point rather than an omission. The lease wants the tracking ref as you last saw it, and going to the network first would ask git to guard you against a change you just accepted sight unseen. A branch with no shared copy gets one, tracking set in the same step. One somebody deleted is put back: typing the verb is saying that out loud. `ff publish --dry-run` says which of those pushes this would be without sending it, and a held rewrite blocks the exit exactly as before.

**A push now leaves a mark**

`ff publish` used to record nothing, and three things went wrong because of it — all reproduced against a real bare remote. fufu reversed your undo and called it advice: publish, `ff undo`, and status said "1 to sync" while `ff sync` fast-forwarded the undone commit straight back. `ff op log` showed no pushes at all, the one irreversible act being the one act it did not record. And a fresh clone of an empty remote reported a loss that never happened.

A push now leaves two marks. The first is a note on the operation log — a note marks something that *happened* rather than something that was *done*, so `ff undo` steps over it and `ff op revert` refuses it. It is written after the push rather than write-ahead, because a remote is not observable without the network and an append-before would be unfalsifiable.

The second is a ref, and it exists because the note alone does not survive the case it was written for: `ff undo` is a pointer move, and everything above the landing leaves the chain, publish notes included. That is correct for the log and exactly wrong for this question, since undo is precisely the thing that cannot reach the wire. The ref sits outside the tracked prefixes so reconcile never reports the push as foreign motion, it pins its commit through a `git gc --prune=now`, and it survives a full `ff trim` — trim drops the log's history, not the fact of where the remote stands.

**Content, not counts**

`ff diff` shows the open change as a patch. `ff show [<rev>]` shows one revision: header and patch, `@` when you name nothing. Both take paths, both speak the same pathspec every other fufu verb does, and both have a `--json` shape.

The diff engine reads down to the line now rather than stopping at the file. `-p` rides `ff evolog`, `ff op show` and `ff op diff` — all three already computed the counts, so the flag is a depth rather than a rendering, and `--json` carries the hunks with it. Without it every one of those payloads is byte-identical to what it was. There is deliberately no `-p` on `ff status`: `ff diff` *is* `ff status -p`, and the page says so.

Short commit hashes are eight characters, decided in one place instead of five.

**The path axis**

`ff log <paths>` answers what happened to a file, and it follows renames by default — a rename boundary runs one tree diff at the boundary rather than a comparison per commit, and the walk is ordered so a parent is never visited before its children, which is the guarantee git's own `--follow` is documented as lacking.

You never type `--`. git needs the separator because one slot takes both revisions and paths; here revisions go to `-r` and the positional is only ever paths, so `ff log main` means the path `main`. A path that names nothing is refused rather than answered with an empty log, and when the token has spaces in it the refusal leads with `ff commit -m "..."`, because a sentence in a path slot is almost always a forgotten flag.

`ff commit <paths>` lands a slice and leaves the rest open. This is the coarse form of what DESIGN already promised — selection at commit time, a choice made once rather than a state maintained — and it reintroduces no index: there is still no state between commits, only an argument at the moment of the close. The unselected edits stay in the working tree and remain the open change, which `ff undo` restores along with everything else.

**Where you can go back to**

`ff op log` answers what happened. `ff history` answers the other question, the one a person actually has when they open a log: where can I go back to? One row is one keystroke — `@` is where the repository stands, each row below is one more press of `ff undo`, each row above one more press of `ff redo` — and a run of captures collapses into the single row it undoes as, carrying its count. Both halves read the same functions `ff undo` and `ff redo` walk with, so the verb and the view cannot describe different futures.

That let `ff op log` become honestly complete. `--captures` is gone: it was a bespoke filter for a concept the revset language already owned, and the two contradicted each other — `ff op log 'kind(capture)'` returned "no operations recorded yet" because the flag silently overrode the expression. The revset is the argument now rather than a flag, and the operation log's read verbs capture first like every other verb, so `@` means now on them too.

`ff version` is its own verb, saying which fufu this is and whether it is current; the flag is lowercase `-v`, and `-V` is answered with the spelling rather than a parse error.

**Starting from fufu**

A new user's first command was `git clone`, so the very first thing fufu taught was that fufu is not the thing you reach for.

`ff init` leaves a repository where the gc guard is written before anything can expire and `ff undo` already has a floor to land on, rather than one that begins whenever some later verb happens to take a capture. Run inside a repository that already exists it means *turn fufu on here* — the same work, reported honestly as already done when it was, which is the adopt path for a repository git made.

`ff clone` is that plus fufu owning the sequence. It is not a wrapper: the negotiation, the pack and the checkout all happen in-process, and the report is in fufu's vocabulary rather than git's. It is also where the shared-copy memory `ff publish` reads starts out true instead of inferred.

**Smaller things**

The map got its shape and its columns right. Bare `ff` on a merge-heavy trunk used to draw nearly every walked commit, because the old rule kept every merge and every topological fork — on a trunk built from merged PRs that is almost everything. It shows branches relative to other branches now: a row is a selected tip, a join where one shown branch's history parts from another's, a merge that lands a shown branch, or a root. And its commit rows carry the same operation id `ff log` and `ff status` put on them, while a clean open change says `no changes` there like it does everywhere else.

`ff git` translation is opt-in. `fufu.translate` defaults to false, so every invocation runs real git verbatim and capture-first; `ff config translate true` restores the old behavior exactly, strict whitelist and all.

Every coded failure names a way out. 99 of the workspace's `Error::coded` raise sites passed an empty exit list, most of them with a way out written down the whole time one lookup away — `ff explain branch/not-found` has always said `ff branch list` while the failure itself said only that the branch was missing. The exits belong to the id now, so the `try:` block, the JSON envelope and `ff explain` all print the same thing, and an id with nothing to type at least names the lookup.

`ff merge`, `ff blame` and `ff tag` join the words fufu answers rather than refuses — each naming what fufu does instead, and the `ff git` spelling that still runs the real thing.

CI runs green on all three platforms with a bench gate that stops coin-flipping, and Windows gets the 8 MiB main stack the other two already have.

`ff explain` grew from 86 error ids to 96. 1191 tests, up from 1043 at v0.5.0.
